l: expulsion of the Carians by Mopsus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The expulsion of the Carians by Mopsus followed the settlement of Rhacius and Manto at Claros. Mopsus, their son, drove the Carians out altogether.

l: depopulation of Colophon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The depopulation of Colophon was carried out by Lysimachus, as previously described in the account of Lysimachus. The inhabitants were transferred as colonists to Ephesus, where they alone among the colonists fought Lysimachus and the Macedonians.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: The unit describes Samos and Chios as Ionian cities and recounts the traditions concerning their rulers, colonists, and earlier inhabitants. Procles led Ionian colonists to Samos, but Androclus and the Ephesians later expelled the Samians, some of whom settled at Samothrace and Anæa before recovering Samos. It also discusses the temple of Hera in Samos, the artists Smilis and Dædalus, and traditions about Hera’s birth and statue. For Chios, Ion the Tragedian records stories of Poseidon and Chios, while later rulers fought the Carians and Abantes and joined the Ionians in sacrifices to the Pan-Ionic league.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: The Ionians inhabited Samos and Chios among the islands. They colonized Samos under Procles, and the community of the Ionians later honored Hector of Chios with a tripod for his prowess.

l: Samos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Samos was inhabited by Ionian colonists who were received by its inhabitants more from necessity than goodwill. After the Samians were expelled, some settled at Samothrace and others at Anæa, and the Samians later recovered the island from the Ephesians.

l: Chios, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Chios was an Ionian city opposite Mimas. Its traditions included the story that Poseidon fathered Chios there, and its rulers Œnopion, Amphiclus, and Hector were associated with Cretan, Eubœan, Carian, and Abantes populations.

l: Procles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Procles, the son of Pityreus and an Epidaurian, led the Ionian colonists to Samos. He was descended from Ion the son of Xuthus, and his son Leogorus succeeded him as king of Samos.

l: Hera, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Hera was believed by the Samians to have been born on Samos beside the river Imbrasus and under the willow-tree that still grew in her temple. The Argonauts were said by some to have brought her statue from Argos.

l: the temple of Hera in Samos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: The temple of Hera in Samos was traditionally said by some to have been built by the Argonauts. Its statue of Hera was made by the Æginetan Smilis, who went to Samos and made the statue there.

l: Dædalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Dædalus was an Athenian of the Metionidæ and was renowned for his art and misfortunes. After killing his sister’s son, he fled to Minos and Crete, later escaped from prison with his son, and went to Cocalus in Sicily, where his art led Cocalus’s daughters to plot against Minos.

l: Ion the Tragedian, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Ion the Tragedian recorded that Poseidon visited unoccupied Chios, had an intrigue with a Nymph, and named their son Chios because snow fell during the birth. He also recorded the succession of Œnopion and his sons, Amphiclus, and Hector, but did not explain how the Chians came to be ranked as Ionians.

l: Pan-Ionic confederacy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: After Hector and the Chians completed their war against the Abantes and Carians, Hector proposed that he and the Ionians should jointly sacrifice for the welfare of the Pan-Ionic league.

l: Ionian colonization of Samos and Chios, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Ionian colonization of Samos was led by Procles, whose followers included many Epidaurians banished from Epidauria. Chios was later associated with Amphiclus, who came from Histiæa in Eubœa in accordance with an oracle at Delphi, though the text does not state how the Chians were ranked as Ionians.

l: the expulsion and recovery of Samos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IV.
s: Androclus and the Ephesians defeated Leogorus, drove the Samians from Samos on the pretext that they had plotted with the Carians, and occupied the island. Some expelled Samians settled at Samothrace and others built a fort at Anæa; ten years later, those under Leogorus crossed back to Samos, expelled the Ephesians, and recovered the island.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The unit describes Smyrna's history, including its capture from the Æolians, its admission to the Pan-Ionic league, and its relocation to the site of modern Smyrna after Alexander the son of Philip received a dream. It surveys Ionia's fertile land, major temples, baths, rivers, groves, caves, and other notable places. It recounts the traditions surrounding the temple of Hercules at Erythræ, its wooden raft, and the fisherman Phormio. It also records local traditions connected with the river Meles, Homer, and other Ionian wonders.

l: Smyrna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Smyrna was one of the twelve cities of the Æolians on the site called the old city, but it was taken by Ionians from Colophon and later admitted to the Pan-Ionic league. Its inhabitants were relocated to the modern city after an oracle at Claros approved the move, and the people of Smyrna worship two Nemeses. In Pausanias's time, Smyrna also had a temple of Æsculapius between Mount Coryphe and the sea.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Ionians took Smyrna from the Æolians and later admitted its inhabitants to the Pan-Ionic league. They possessed a fertile country with magnificent temples and many notable natural and cultural sites.

l: Alexander the son of Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Alexander the son of Philip built modern Smyrna after receiving a dream while returning from hunting on Mount Pagus. He was directed to establish the town at the site of the dream and move the people of Smyrna there.

l: Mount Pagus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Mount Pagus was the place from which Alexander the son of Philip returned while hunting before visiting the temple of Nemesis. Modern Smyrna was built on its site or in its vicinity.

l: Nemesis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Nemesis appeared to Alexander the son of Philip in a dream, together with another goddess, and instructed him to build a town and relocate Smyrna's inhabitants. The people of Smyrna worshiped two Nemeses and said that their mother was Night, while the Athenians at Rhamnus said Nemesis was the daughter of Oceanus.

l: Alexander's dream, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Alexander's dream occurred after he returned from hunting on Mount Pagus and slept beneath a plane-tree growing in the water before the temple of Nemesis. The goddesses of Nemesis appeared in the dream and told him to build a town there and move Smyrna's people from the old city.

l: relocation of Smyrna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The people of Smyrna consulted the oracle at Claros about relocating from the old city. They willingly moved after receiving the response that those living near Mount Pagus across the sacred Meles would be thrice and four times happy.

l: Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Claros was the place to which the people of Smyrna sent envoys to consult the oracle about their situation. It also contained a temple of Apollo in Colophonia that was not quite finished.

l: oracle of Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The oracle of Claros responded to Smyrna's consultation with a prophecy praising those who would dwell near Mount Pagus across the sacred Meles. The response encouraged the people of Smyrna to relocate.

l: Ionia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Ionia was praised for its fertile land, healthy air, temples, baths, rivers, groves, caves, and other wonders. Its notable places included sites at Ephesus, Miletus, Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Clazomenæ, Erythræ, Smyrna, Chios, and Samos.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Ephesian Artemis had the finest temple in Ionia in size and opulence.

l: Erythræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Erythræ possessed a temple of Hercules, a temple of Athene Polias, and a notable ancient work of art. It also had Chalcis, a promontory and sea baths considered the most beneficial in Ionia.

l: temple of Hercules at Erythræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The temple of Hercules at Erythræ was admired for its great antiquity and contained a wooden raft associated with the god's voyage from Tyre in Phœnicia. Only Thracian women were allowed to enter it, and the rope made from their hair was still preserved there.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Hercules was associated with a wooden raft said to have sailed from Tyre in Phœnicia to Erythræ. His temple there was considered exceptionally ancient.

l: wooden raft of Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The wooden raft of Hercules was said to have sailed from Tyre and to have reached the Ionian sea after being moored at the promontory called Mid. The people of Erythræ and Chios struggled to bring it ashore until a rope made from the hair of Thracian women enabled them to do so.

l: Phormio, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Phormio was a blind fisherman from Erythræ who dreamed that the women should cut off their hair and that the men should make a rope from it to drag the raft ashore. After the raft was brought to land, he recovered his sight and remained able to see for the rest of his life.

l: river Meles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The sacred Meles was named in the oracle of Claros as lying across from Mount Pagus. Near Smyrna, the river Meles was described as exceptionally beautiful.

l: cave near the springs of Meles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: A cave near the springs of the Meles was said to be the place where Homer wrote his Poems.

l: Homer, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: Homer was traditionally said to have written his Poems in a cave near the springs of the river Meles at Smyrna.

l: Ionian temples and wonders, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER V.
s: The Ionian temples and wonders included the temple of Ephesian Artemis, unfinished temples of Apollo at Branchidæ and Claros, temples at Samos, Phocæa, Erythræ, and Priene, and numerous baths, rivers, groves, caves, tombs, and sacred sites. They were described as nearly equal to the wonders of Greece as a whole.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: After the Ionians departed, the Achæans divided their land among twelve towns, including Patræ, and were ruled by several kings and powerful families. The Achæans participated in the Trojan War and later fought in some Greek wars, but they did not join the Greek forces at Thermopylæ, Salamis, or Platæa during the invasion of Greece by Xerxes and the Medes. They later allied with Patræ and the Athenians against the Lacedæmonians and took part in the war at Chæronea against Philip and the Macedonians, though they did not fight at Lamia. After the Galati crossed into Asia Minor, no Greek state clearly remained dominant because Lacedæmon, Thebes, and the Athenians had each been weakened.

l: Ionians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Ionians departed from the land that the Achæans then divided among twelve towns. Those towns had formerly been inhabited by the Ionians.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Achæans settled in twelve towns and were ruled by kings and powerful families, including the sons of Tisamenus and Damasias. They supplied the largest contingent from Greece in Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium, but later remained absent from Thermopylæ, the sea-fights near Eubœa and Salamis, and Platæa. They allied with Patræ and the Athenians against the Lacedæmonians, fought at Chæronea against Philip and the Macedonians, and did not fight at Lamia because they had not recovered from their reverse in Bœotia.

l: Lacedæmon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Lacedæmon was one of the regions inhabited by the Achæans during Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium. Its later reverse at Leuctra, the rise of Megalopolis, and the proximity of the Messenians prevented it from recovering its former prosperity.

l: Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Patræ was a city built in Achæan territory by Preugenes and his son Patreus from Lacedæmon, and it was named after Patreus. The Achæans later allied themselves with the people of Patræ against the Lacedæmonians and were friendly with the Athenians.

l: Trojan War, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: During Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium in the Trojan War, the Achæans provided the largest contingent from Greece because they inhabited both Lacedæmon and Argos.

l: Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Achæans did not join Leonidas at the pass of Thermopylæ during the invasion of Greece by Xerxes and the Medes. The pass was later overlooked by the Peloponnesians and the Achæans when the Galati invaded, because they believed the Isthmus of Corinth was sufficiently fortified.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Athenians fought under Themistocles in the sea-fights off Eubœa and Salamis and later had the good will of Greece because of their famous actions. The Achæans were friendly with them and fought alongside them in a later war against the Lacedæmonians, but Athenian goodwill did not secure victory in their war with the Macedonians.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: Greece was invaded by Xerxes and the Medes, but the Achæans did not join the principal Greek forces in that invasion. After the Galati crossed into Asia Minor, no Greek state was clearly the leading power.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Achæans fought against Philip and the Macedonians at Chæronea. The Athenians later fought a war with the Macedonians, and their goodwill throughout Greece did not guarantee them security in that conflict.

l: Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Galati crossed into Asia Minor in ships after passing through the undefended route at Thermopylæ. Their migration contributed to a situation in which no Greek state was clearly dominant.

l: Peloponnesians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Peloponnesians, including the Achæans, overlooked the pass at Thermopylæ when the Galati advanced because they believed the barbarians could not threaten them by sea and that the Isthmus of Corinth was strongly fortified.

l: wars of the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Achæans fought in Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium, later allied with Patræ and the Athenians against the Lacedæmonians, and fought at Chæronea against Philip and the Macedonians. They did not join the battles at Thermopylæ, Salamis, or Platæa during Xerxes’ invasion, and they did not fight at Lamia.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: During the invasion of Greece by Xerxes and the Medes, the Achæans did not join Leonidas at Thermopylæ, the forces of Themistocles and the Athenians at Salamis, or the allied forces at Platæa. The text suggests that they stayed behind to protect their country.

l: Galatian migration into Asia Minor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Galatian migration into Asia Minor began when the Galati crossed over in ships after the pass at Thermopylæ had been left unguarded. Their arrival coincided with the weakening of the principal Greek states and the absence of a clearly leading power in Greece.

l: war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VI.
s: During the war between the Lacedæmonians and Athenians, the Achæans readily allied themselves with the people of Patræ and were equally friendly with the Athenians.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Achæans formed the Achæan League at Ægium, and the Sicyonians and other Peloponnesians later joined it as its power grew. The Lacedæmonians opposed the Achæans, with Agis capturing Pellene briefly and Cleomenes later defeating the Achæans before making and breaking peace with them and Antigonus. Antigonus governed the Macedonians as regent for Philip, the son of Demetrius, who later took power and established garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis, and Magnesia while attacking the Athenians and Ætolians. Rome intervened against Philip by sending an army under Otilius, who captured and destroyed Hestiæa and Anticyra, leading the Senate to replace him with Flaminius.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Achæans were especially powerful when the Greeks were not united, and their towns had largely escaped tyrannies, wars, and plague. They formed the Achæan League, fought the Lacedæmonians, and with Antigonus defeated them at Sellasia after Cleomenes violated his agreements.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Achæan League was formed by common consent at Ægium. The Sicyonians joined first, followed by other Peloponnesians, and its growing power encouraged people outside the Isthmus to join.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Lacedæmonians were the only Greeks described as unfriendly to the Achæans and openly took up arms against them. Their forces suffered defeat at Sellasia at the hands of the Achæans and Antigonus after Cleomenes broke his word.

l: Aratus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Aratus and the Sicyonians drove Agis, the son of Eudamidas, out of Pellene after Agis had captured the town. Aratus and the Achæans were later badly defeated by Cleomenes at Dyme.

l: Antigonus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Antigonus was ruler of the Macedonians as regent for Philip, the son of Demetrius, and was Philip's uncle and stepfather. He made peace with Cleomenes and the Achæans, later defeated the Lacedæmonians with the Achæans at Sellasia, and surrendered rule to Philip when Philip came of age.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Macedonians were ruled by Antigonus as regent for Philip, the son of Demetrius, until Philip came of age. Under Philip, they maintained garrison positions at Corinth, Chalcis, and Magnesia as bases against Greece.

l: Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Philip, the son of Demetrius, received rule over the Macedonians from his stepfather Antigonus when he came of age. He imitated Philip the son of Amyntas, used bribery and poison, established garrison towns called the keys of Greece, and raided the Athenians and Ætolians.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Athenians were harassed by Philip's repeated raids and plundering incursions. Because their allies were weak, they relied on an alliance with Rome, and Otilius was ordered to protect them against Philip.

l: Ætolians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Ætolians were among those especially harassed by Philip's raids. Roman forces were nominally sent to assist them against Philip and were later ordered to protect them.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Greeks were initially not banded together, allowing the Achæans to become powerful through their League. Philip established fortified garrisons as the keys of Greece and carried out raids against Greek communities.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Romans first sent soldiers nominally to assist the Ætolians against Philip but really to observe Macedonian aims. They later sent an army under Otilius to protect the Athenians and Ætolians, and their Senate replaced Otilius after his unauthorized destruction of Hestiæa and Anticyra.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Rome formed an alliance with the Athenians because their other allies were weak. It intervened militarily against Philip by sending forces to assist or protect the Ætolians and Athenians.

l: Roman Otilius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Otilius, the best-known name of the Roman commander, was ordered to protect the Athenians and Ætolians against Philip. Although he otherwise obeyed his orders, he captured and razed Hestiæa and Anticyra, which had submitted to Philip out of necessity, and was then superseded by Flaminius.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Greece was threatened by Philip's fortified garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis, and Magnesia, which he called its keys. Philip also harassed Greek communities through continual raids and plundering incursions.

l: Achæan League formation, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Achæan League was formed at Ægium because the town had been prominent in Achaia and was then its most powerful town, following Helice's destruction by a flood. The Sicyonians joined first, and other Peloponnesians followed immediately or later.

l: Philip's accession to rule over the Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: Philip, the son of Demetrius, took rule over the Macedonians from his stepfather Antigonus when he came of age. Antigonus was willing to surrender the rule, while Philip soon caused fear among the Greeks through his methods and military policies.

l: Roman military intervention against Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Romans first sent soldiers to assist the Ætolians nominally while investigating Macedonian intentions, then sent an army under Otilius to protect the Athenians and Ætolians against Philip. Otilius's destruction of Hestiæa and Anticyra displeased the Roman Senate, which replaced him with Flaminius.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Flaminius defeated the Macedonian garrison at Eretria, besieged Corinth, and urged the Achæans to join the Romans. The Achæans eventually joined the siege, and Corinth joined the Achæan League after being freed from the Macedonian garrison. The Achæans later supported the Romans against Philip, the Ætolians, and Antiochus, while imposing severe measures on Sparta after Nabis was overthrown. Philip suffered a decisive defeat at Cynoscephalæ and was forced by the Roman peace terms to withdraw his garrisons from the Greek towns he had seized.

l: Flaminius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Flaminius defeated the Macedonian garrison at Eretria, plundered the town, and then besieged Corinth. He urged the Achæans to join the Romans and later defeated Philip and the Macedonians at Cynoscephalæ.

l: Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Corinth was occupied by Philip’s garrison and was besieged by Flaminius. After the Macedonian garrison was overcome, Corinth joined the Achæan League.

l: Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Philip’s garrison held Eretria and Corinth, but he was defeated by Flaminius and the Romans at Cynoscephalæ. He lost most of his army and was required to remove his garrisons from the Greek towns seized during the war.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Achæans initially resented the Romans’ harsh treatment of old Greek cities and feared replacing Macedonian rule with Roman domination. They eventually joined Flaminius in the siege of Corinth, became allies of the Romans, fought with them against Philip, the Ætolians, and Antiochus, and imposed severe measures on the Lacedæmonians.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Romans defeated Philip and the Macedonian Empire and became allies of the Achæans. They also fought against the Ætolians and Antiochus and required Philip to withdraw his garrisons from Greek towns.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Flaminius sought the Achæans as allies of the Romans and as friends to the Greeks generally. Philip was required to remove his garrisons from Greek towns that he had seized during the war.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Macedonians fought Flaminius and the Romans at Cynoscephalæ and were decisively defeated. Their supremacy received a fatal blow, and their garrisons had to be withdrawn from the Greek towns seized during the war.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Achæan League received Corinth after the city was freed from the Macedonian garrison. It later included the Lacedæmonians, dealt severely with them, and forced their youths to train in the Achæan manner.

l: Ætolians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Ætolians were opposed by the Romans and the Achæans. The Achæans fought against them partly to satisfy a long-standing grudge.

l: Nabis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Nabis is described as a man of extreme cruelty whose power at Sparta was overthrown. After his power ended, the Lacedæmonians became their own masters again before being brought into the Achæan League.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: After Nabis was overthrown, the Lacedæmonians became independent again but were later brought into the Achæan League. The Achæans destroyed Sparta’s fortifications, prevented its youths from training according to Lycurgus, and made them train in the Achæan way; the Lacedæmonians then sought the support of Metellus and his colleagues.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Sparta’s fortifications, strengthened during the power of Nabis, were destroyed by the Achæans. The Achæans also interfered with the training of its youths.

l: Macedonian supremacy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Macedonian supremacy received a fatal blow from the Romans after Philip’s defeat at Cynoscephalæ. The text connects its collapse with the defeat of the later Philip.

l: battle of Cynoscephalæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: At the battle of Cynoscephalæ, Philip fought Flaminius and the Romans and was badly defeated. He lost most of his army and was forced to accept terms requiring the removal of his garrisons from Greek towns.

l: Cynoscephalæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Cynoscephalæ was the range of hills where Philip and the Macedonians were defeated by Flaminius and the Romans.

l: Roman-Macedonian peace, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The peace obtained by Philip from the Romans sounded impressive but was secured through entreaties and great expenditure of money. Its terms required him to remove his garrisons from the Greek towns he had seized and reduced during the war.

l: Roman capture and destruction of Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: Flaminius began a regular siege of Corinth after defeating the Macedonian garrison at Eretria. The Achæans eventually joined the siege, and Corinth then joined the Achæan League.

l: Roman expedition against Macedonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER VIII.
s: The Romans, supported by the Achæans, fought against Philip and the Macedonians. Their victory at Cynoscephalæ dealt a fatal blow to Macedonian supremacy and forced Philip to withdraw his garrisons from the Greek towns.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Metellus and his colleagues urged the Achæans to treat the Lacedæmonians more kindly, but the Achæans refused to hear them without a decree from the Roman Senate. After Metellus reported against the Achæans, Areus and Alcibiades also denounced them before the Senate, prompting further Roman intervention. Appius and later a larger Roman delegation restored exiled Lacedæmonians, remitted certain fines, and altered the jurisdiction of capital cases while leaving Sparta in the Achæan League. The restored Lacedæmonians then encouraged Messenian and Achæan exiles to appeal to Rome, and the Senate ordered their restoration, which deeply embittered the Achæans.

l: Metellus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Metellus and his colleagues urged the Achæans to treat the Lacedæmonians more kindly. When the Achæans refused to hear them without a decree from the Roman Senate, Metellus returned to Rome and reported many things against the Achæans, some of which were untrue.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Lacedæmonians were the subject of a dispute with the Achæans. Roman intervention restored exiles to Sparta, remitted certain fines, left them in the Achæan League, and allowed them to send envoys to Rome.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Achæans refused to hear Roman advice about the Lacedæmonians without a decree from the Roman Senate. They sentenced Areus and Alcibiades to death, resisted Roman decisions, and ultimately submitted to measures restoring exiles and changing the jurisdiction of capital cases.

l: Roman Senate, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Roman Senate heard accusations against the Achæans from Metellus, Areus, and Alcibiades. It sent Appius and others to settle the dispute, later authorized a plenipotentiary mission, and ordered Athens and Ætolia to restore Messenian and Achæan exiles to their rights.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Romans intervened repeatedly in the quarrel between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians. Their actions favored the Lacedæmonians and exiles in the Achæans’ view, despite the Achæans’ past services against Philip, the Ætolians, and Antiochus.

l: Areus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Areus, a prominent man at Sparta, had been exiled by Nabis and kindly received by the Achæans, who later helped restore him to Sparta against the wishes of the Lacedæmonian people. He denounced the Achæans before the Roman Senate, was included in Appius’ suite, and was declared by Appius’ delegation to have committed no crime against them.

l: Alcibiades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Alcibiades had been exiled by Nabis and received and restored by the Achæans. He later denounced the Achæans before the Roman Senate, accompanied Appius, and was declared by Appius’ delegation to have committed no crime against them.

l: Appius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Appius was sent by the Roman Senate to settle the differences between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians. He and his suite provoked the Achæans, supported Areus and Alcibiades, favored the Lacedæmonians, and secured decisions restoring exiles and remitting fines.

l: Lycortas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Lycortas, described as second to none among the Arcadians and as friendly with Philopœmen, defended the just claims of the Achæans before the council. In doing so, he also covertly criticized the Romans.

l: Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Philopœmen is mentioned as a person with whom Lycortas had friendly relations and upon whom Lycortas relied. The text also refers to Messenians involved in Philopœmen’s death.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Sparta received back Lacedæmonians who had been exiled by the Achæans. The Spartans rebuilt walls around the city from the foundation.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Romans did not remove the Lacedæmonians from the Achæan League. They ordered that foreign, understood as Roman, courts try capital cases, while other cases could be tried by the Lacedæmonians themselves or submitted to the Achæan League.

l: Roman embassy to the Achæans and Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The embassy led by Appius was sent to place the differences between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians on a just footing. Its members supported the Lacedæmonians, restored exiles, remitted fines of people condemned in their absence, and authorized Lacedæmonian envoys to go to Rome.

l: murder of Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The Messenians involved in the death of Philopœmen were thought to have been banished by the Achæans for that reason. The restored Lacedæmonians encouraged them and other Achæan exiles to appeal to Rome.

l: differences between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: The differences concerned the treatment and status of the Lacedæmonians within the Achæan League, the return of exiles, fines, and judicial authority. Roman interventions settled these matters in ways that the Achæans regarded as unjust and increasingly favorable to the Lacedæmonians.

l: restoration of exiles and remission of fines, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER IX.
s: Appius and his fellow plenipotentiaries restored to Sparta those exiled by the Achæans and remitted the fines of people who had fled before judgment and been condemned in their absence. The restored Lacedæmonians then promoted appeals by Messenian and Achæan exiles, and the Roman Senate ordered their restoration to their rights.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The text presents betrayal of one’s country and fellow citizens for gain as a recurring cause of destruction in Greece, culminating in the subjection of the Achæans to the Romans through Callicrates. Perseus the son of Philip violated his agreement with the Romans by attacking Abrupolis, king of the Sapæans, whose people were Roman allies, leading to war and the overthrow of Perseus and the Macedonian Empire. After the war, Roman Senators accused prominent Achæans of aiding Perseus, and Callicrates helped secure the dispatch of more than 1,000 Achæans to Rome for trial. The Romans imprisoned them in various towns in Etruria and released only about 300 or fewer 17 years later.

l: betrayal of one’s country and fellow citizens for gain, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The text calls betrayal of one’s country and fellow citizens for gain the most impious of crimes and says it repeatedly troubled and weakened Greece. It gives examples involving the Samians, Eretria, Thessaly, Thebes, Elis, and other Greek cities.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Achæans were made entirely subject to the Romans through the actions of Callicrates. More than 1,000 Achæans accused of being friendly to Perseus were sent to Rome, imprisoned in Etruria, and only about 300 or fewer were later released.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Greece suffered repeated destruction through treason, and its cities were said to have been ruined by treason more than formerly by the plague. After the Romans defeated Perseus, the Achæans became subject to Rome.

l: Philip the son of Amyntas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: During the reign of Philip, the son of Amyntas, many Greek cities were betrayed, and Lacedæmon was not the only city affected. The text also contrasts his treatment of Greek opponents with the later Roman practice of sending accused Achæans to Rome.

l: Lamia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: After the reverse to the Greeks at Lamia, Antipater wanted to cross quickly to the war in Asia Minor and was willing to make a rapid peace. At Lamia, although only 200 Greeks fell, the Athenians became slaves of the Macedonians.

l: Antipater, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: After the Greek reverse at Lamia, Antipater wished to proceed quickly to the war in Asia Minor. He was initially content to arrange a speedy peace, since he did not regard it as important whether Athens or all Greece remained free, but Demades and other Athenian traitors persuaded him to act otherwise.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: After the reverse in Bœotia, Athens did not become subject to Philip, although 1,000 were killed and 2,000 taken prisoner. After Lamia, Demades and other traitors helped bring Macedonian garrisons into Athens, and the Athenians became slaves of the Macedonians.

l: Perseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Perseus was initially at peace with the Romans under the agreement made with his father, Philip, but violated it by leading an army against Abrupolis, king of the Sapæans, and dispossessing them. He and the Macedonians were defeated in war because of this action.

l: Macedonian supremacy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Macedonian Empire was overthrown by the Romans along with Perseus. Its defeat marked the beginning of the troubles that eventually made the Achæans entirely subject to Rome.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Romans defeated Perseus and the Macedonian Empire and sent ten Senators to settle affairs in Macedonia according to Roman interests. They ordered accused Achæans to stand trial at Rome, imprisoned them in Etruria, ignored Achæan embassies and supplications, and later released only some of the survivors.

l: Roman Senators, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Ten Roman Senators were sent to settle affairs in Macedonia after Perseus and the Macedonians were defeated. One Senator, influenced by Callicrates, urged the Achæans to condemn alleged supporters of Perseus and then sent those accused to Rome.

l: Callicrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: Callicrates ingratiated himself with the Roman Senators through flattery and persuaded one Senator to enter the Achæan League. He instigated accusations against prominent Achæans and helped cause more than 1,000 of them to be sent to Rome.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: A Roman Senator entered the Achæan League and addressed one of its general meetings. When the Senator demanded that alleged supporters of Perseus be condemned, Xeno challenged the accusation and offered to stand trial before either the Achæan League or the Romans.

l: Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Macedonians, under Perseus, were defeated in war after Perseus attacked Abrupolis and dispossessed the Sapæans, Roman allies. The Macedonians later held the Athenians in slavery after Lamia.

l: Italy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Romans imprisoned the Achæans they had sent to Rome in various towns in Etruria, and 17 years later only about 300 or fewer of the more than 1,000 remained in Italy.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: A Roman Senator ordered Achæans accused by Callicrates to stand trial at Rome. More than 1,000 went there, although the Romans treated them as already condemned and imprisoned them in towns in Etruria.

l: overthrow of Perseus and the Macedonian Empire by the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The overthrow of Perseus and the Macedonian Empire by the Romans is identified as the beginning of the Achæans’ troubles. It was followed by Roman intervention in Macedonia and the eventual subjection of the Achæans.

l: war between Perseus and the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The war began after Perseus violated his peace agreement with the Romans by attacking Abrupolis, king of the Sapæans, who were Roman allies. Perseus and the Macedonians were defeated because of this outrage.

l: trial of the Achæans at Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The trial of the Achæans at Rome followed accusations by Callicrates and a Roman Senator that prominent Achæans had supported Perseus. More than 1,000 Achæans were sent to Rome, despite the earlier objection that they should not be condemned before their alleged actions were identified.

l: Achæans imprisoned in Etruria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER X.
s: The Achæans imprisoned in Etruria were treated by the Romans as though they had already been condemned. The Romans ignored repeated Achæan embassies and supplications, then released about 300 or fewer of them 17 years later, considering that they had been punished sufficiently.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Romans sent Gallus to Greece to arbitrate the disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Argives, and authorized him to release towns from the Achæan League. The Athenians plundered Oropus, and the Roman Senate ordered a fine that was later reduced from 500 talents to 100, though the Athenians did not pay it. The Oropians secured an agreement involving an Athenian garrison and hostages, but an outrage by members of the garrison led them to demand compliance. Menalcidas and Callicrates persuaded the Achæans to assist the Oropians, but the Athenians plundered Oropus again and withdrew their garrison before the Achaean army arrived.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Romans sent Gallus to Greece to arbitrate the disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Argives. They consented to the request of the Ætolians who inhabited Pleuron to leave the Achæan League and authorized Gallus to release as many towns from the League as he wished.

l: Roman Senate, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Roman Senate ordered the Sicyonians to impose on the Athenians a fine proportionate to the harm done to the Oropians. At the Athenians’ request, it remitted the fine from 500 talents to 100 talents.

l: Gallus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Gallus was sent to Greece to arbitrate the disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Argives. He treated the Greeks, especially the Lacedæmonians and Argives, with great contempt, and was authorized to release towns from the Achæan League.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Gallus acted with hauteur toward the Greeks and treated the Lacedæmonians and Argives contemptuously. The Athenians were described as having been reduced to greater poverty than any of the Greeks by the war with the Macedonians.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Lacedæmonians were involved in disputes with the Argives that Gallus was sent to arbitrate. Gallus treated them with great contempt, and Lacedæmonians in the Achaean army opposed making an inroad into Attica.

l: Argives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Argives were involved in disputes with the Lacedæmonians that Gallus was sent to arbitrate. Gallus treated them with great contempt.

l: disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Argives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Romans sent Gallus to Greece to arbitrate these disputes. Gallus disdained to arbitrate for the Lacedæmonians and Argives and treated them contemptuously.

l: Callicrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Callicrates was described as the plague of all Greece and as having great influence over the Achæans because of his friendship with the Romans. Menalcidas promised him half of the payment offered by the Oropians, and Callicrates helped bring about the decision to assist them.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Gallus was authorized to release towns from the Achæan League. The Ætolians who inhabited Pleuron were allowed to send a private embassy to Rome to seek release and received Roman consent.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Athenians, driven by poverty after the war with the Macedonians, plundered Oropus. They did not pay the 100-talent fine imposed after the raid, made an agreement involving a garrison and hostages, later refused to comply when the Oropians demanded it, and plundered Oropus again before withdrawing their garrison.

l: Oropus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Oropus was a town subject to the Athenians. The Athenians plundered it twice, and an Athenian garrison occupied it for a time before withdrawing.

l: Oropians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Oropians appealed to the Roman Senate after the Athenians plundered Oropus. They agreed to an arrangement involving an Athenian garrison and hostages, but later demanded the return of the hostages and removal of the garrison after an outrage. They promised ten talents to Menalcidas to obtain Achaean assistance.

l: plundering of Oropus by the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Athenians first plundered Oropus out of necessity rather than choice because of their poverty. After the Achaean army was summoned to help the Oropians, the Athenians returned, plundered what they had spared in their first raid, and withdrew their garrison.

l: fine imposed on the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Sicyonians fined the Athenians 500 talents in their absence for the harm done to the Oropians. The Roman Senate remitted all but 100 talents, and the Athenians did not pay the remaining amount.

l: Athenian garrison at Oropus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Under the agreement with the Oropians, an Athenian garrison occupied Oropus. After an outrage by some members of the garrison, the Oropians demanded its removal, and the Athenians eventually withdrew it after plundering Oropus again.

l: agreement between the Athenians and Oropians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The agreement provided that an Athenian garrison would occupy Oropus and that the Athenians would hold hostages from the Oropians. If the Oropians brought further charges against the Athenians, the Athenians were to withdraw the garrison and return the hostages.

l: outrage by members of the Athenian garrison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Some members of the Athenian garrison insulted townsmen of Oropus. The Oropians cited this outrage when they demanded the return of their hostages and the removal of the garrison.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Achæans initially refused the Oropians’ request for help out of friendship and respect for the Athenians. After Menalcidas and Callicrates supported assistance, an Achaean army came too late to help, and it rejected their proposal to invade Attica.

l: Menalcidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Menalcidas was a Lacedæmonian by birth and was serving as General of the Achæans. He promised Callicrates half of the ten talents offered by the Oropians if he would help secure Achaean assistance, and he later tried to persuade the Achaean army to invade Attica.

l: promise of payment to Menalcidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Oropians promised Menalcidas ten talents if he would make the Achæans help them. Menalcidas promised half of this money to Callicrates.

l: Oropian appeal for Achaean assistance, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Oropians appealed to the Achæans for help after the Athenians refused to return the hostages and remove the garrison. The Achæans initially refused, but the Oropians then offered Menalcidas ten talents, after which assistance was decided upon.

l: Roman decision to assist the Oropians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: The Roman Senate responded to the Oropians’ appeal by ordering the Sicyonians to impose a fine on the Athenians. It reduced the fine from 500 talents to 100 talents at the Athenians’ request.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Athens was the city whose people plundered Oropus and refused to fulfill the agreement after the garrison’s outrage. Menalcidas and Callicrates later tried to persuade the Achæans to invade Attica.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XI.
s: Rome was the place where the Oropians appealed to the Senate and where the Ætolians who inhabited Pleuron were allowed to send a private embassy. The Romans and the Senate made decisions concerning the Achæan League and the fine imposed on the Athenians.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Oropians paid Menalcidas, who withheld Callicrates's share, prompting Callicrates to prosecute him before the Achæans. Menalcidas bribed Diæus of Megalopolis with three talents to secure his acquittal, and Diæus then misrepresented the Roman Senate's instructions concerning Spartan jurisdiction. Disputes over those instructions led to war between the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians, while prominent Spartans went into exile and were condemned in their absence. The Roman Senate said it would send ambassadors to arbitrate, but their delayed arrival allowed Diæus and Menalcidas to deceive the Achæans and Lacedæmonians respectively.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Achæans received no help from their side in the Oropian affair, but Menalcidas and Diæus acted in ways that angered them. They prosecuted Menalcidas, were vexed by Diæus's securing his acquittal, disputed the Lacedæmonians' right to consult Rome privately, and were later deceived by Diæus about the Roman Senate's instructions.

l: Menalcidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Menalcidas received the money promised by the Oropians but tried to keep Callicrates from receiving his share and ultimately deprived him of it. Callicrates prosecuted him before the Achæans, so Menalcidas bribed Diæus with three talents from Oropus to obtain his acquittal. He later disputed bitterly with Diæus before the Roman Senate and deceived the Lacedæmonians about the Senate's decision.

l: Callicrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Callicrates was denied his share of the Oropian money by Menalcidas and prosecuted him before the Achæans on a capital charge. He was sent with Diæus to Rome to oppose the Spartan exiles, but died of an illness on the journey.

l: Diæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Diæus, Menalcidas's successor as General of the Achæans, accepted three talents from Menalcidas and worked to secure his acquittal. He falsely told the Achæans that the Roman Senate allowed them to sentence a Spartan to death, opposed referring the matter back to Rome, and later persuaded the Achæans that the Lacedæmonians had been ordered to obey them in all things.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Sparta was the subject of a dispute involving the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians. Diæus claimed he intended to fight for everything troubling Sparta rather than against Sparta itself.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Lacedæmonians consulted the Roman Senate about disputed land and disputed Diæus's account of the Senate's decision. Knowing they could not fight the Achæans, they sent embassies to the cities and spoke privately to Diæus. Menalcidas later deceived them by claiming that Rome had removed them altogether from the jurisdiction of the Achæan League.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Achæan League was involved in the prosecution of Menalcidas and in the conflict with the Lacedæmonians. The Achæans argued that its cities could not send a private embassy to Rome without common consent.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: Rome was the destination of embassies from the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans concerning the dispute. The Roman Senate was said to have directed the Lacedæmonians to try all but capital cases before the Achæan League, and later announced that ambassadors would arbitrate the dispute.

l: Roman Senate, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Roman Senate told the Lacedæmonians to try all but capital cases before the Achæan League. It also received the dispute involving the Spartan exiles and Menalcidas, and answered that it would send ambassadors to arbitrate between the Lacedæmonians and Achæans.

l: the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Roman ambassadors were sent to arbitrate the differences between the Lacedæmonians and Achæans. Their journey from Rome was so leisurely that Diæus and Menalcidas had time to deceive the two sides.

l: the jurisdiction of the Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The jurisdiction of the Achæan League was disputed by the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans. Menalcidas falsely told the Lacedæmonians that Rome had removed them altogether from it.

l: war between the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: War broke out after disputes over whether the Lacedæmonians could pass sentence on themselves and whether the matter could be referred privately to the Roman Senate. The Lacedæmonians believed they were unable to fight the Achæans and sought other means of responding.

l: the Roman arbitration of the Spartan-Achæan dispute, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Roman Senate announced that it would send ambassadors to arbitrate the differences between the Lacedæmonians and Achæans. The arbitration was delayed because the ambassadors traveled from Rome slowly, allowing Diæus and Menalcidas to misrepresent the Senate's decision.

l: the Roman Senate's directive concerning Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XII.
s: The Roman Senate's stated directive was that the Lacedæmonians should try all cases except capital cases before the Achæan League. Diæus falsely represented this as permission for the Achæans to pass sentence of death upon a Spartan, while Menalcidas falsely claimed that the Lacedæmonians had been removed from the League's jurisdiction altogether.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Achæans prepared to renew their war with the Lacedæmonians under Damocritus, while Metellus and the Romans defeated Andriscus in Macedonia and ordered the Achæans to await Roman arbitrators. Damocritus defeated the Lacedæmonians near Sparta but failed to pursue them, was fined 50 talents, and fled when he could not pay. Diæus succeeded him, agreed to delay open warfare, but strengthened the Achæans by securing towns around Sparta and placing garrisons in them. Menalcidas then persuaded the Lacedæmonians to violate the truce and sack Iasus, after which he was accused and committed suicide by poison.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Achæans prepared an army to war against the Lacedæmonians, defeated them in battle, and established friendly relations and garrisons in towns around Sparta. They fined Damocritus 50 talents for failing to pursue his victory.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Lacedæmonians took up arms to defend their country but were defeated, losing about 1,000 men in the battle before the rest fled into Sparta. Later, Menalcidas persuaded them to violate the truce and sack Iasus.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Romans, under Metellus, quickly finished the war in Macedonia against Andriscus. Roman envoys ordered the Achæans not to war against Sparta and to await arbitrators sent from Rome.

l: Damocritus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Damocritus was chosen General of the Achæans and led the army against the Lacedæmonians. Although he defeated them, he recalled the pursuing Achæans and preferred raids and plundering to a regular siege, so the Achæans fined him 50 talents; unable to pay, he fled the Peloponnese.

l: Metellus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Metellus led the Roman army against Andriscus in Macedonia and finished the war with great despatch. He ordered Roman envoys to forbid the Achæans to attack Sparta and to tell them to await the Roman arbitrators.

l: Diæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Diæus succeeded Damocritus as General of the Achæans and agreed, after a second message from Metellus, to wait for the Roman arbitrators rather than continue the war openly. He then won over the towns around Sparta and placed Achæan garrisons in them.

l: Menalcidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Menalcidas was chosen General of the Lacedæmonians and persuaded them to violate the truce because they lacked supplies and money and their land had been uncultivated. He captured and sacked Iasus, was accused by the citizens after renewing the conflict, and committed suicide by poison.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: Sparta was defended by the Lacedæmonians after their defeat in battle, as the surviving army fled into the town. Diæus later surrounded it indirectly by securing nearby towns and placing Achæan garrisons in them.

l: war between the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The war was renewed after differences between the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians, despite Roman orders that the Achæans wait for arbitrators. It continued through the defeat of the Lacedæmonians, the Achæan occupation of nearby towns, and Menalcidas's violation of the truce.

l: battle between the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The battle ended in an Achæan victory, with about 1,000 Lacedæmonians in their prime killed and the rest fleeing into Sparta. Damocritus did not pursue the fugitives to the walls.

l: Achaean army, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIII.
s: The Achaean army marched against Lacedæmon and defeated the Lacedæmonians. It was recalled from pursuing the fleeing enemy and then engaged mainly in raids and plundering rather than a regular siege.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Orestes and other Roman envoys came to Greece to arbitrate the disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans, conveying the Roman Senate’s view that several communities should not be forced into the Achæan League. The Achæans responded by attacking and imprisoning Lacedæmonians at Corinth, while sending ambassadors toward Rome. Critolaus then deceived the Roman commissioners, became General of the Achæans, and persuaded them to undertake war against Sparta and Rome. Pytheas and the Thebans further encouraged the conflict, although the Thebans had recently been fined for invasions and ravages.

l: Orestes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Orestes arrived in Greece among the Roman envoys and summoned Diæus and the principal people of the Achæan cities. He announced the Roman Senate’s position and tried to stop the Achæans from assaulting Lacedæmonians who had taken refuge at his headquarters.

l: Diæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Diæus was summoned before Orestes with the principal Achæans. After serving his time as General of the Achæans, he was succeeded by Critolaus.

l: Critolaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Critolaus succeeded Diæus as General of the Achæans and was possessed by an unreasoning desire to fight the Romans. He deceived the Roman envoys at Tegea, collected an Achæan army at Corinth, and persuaded it to war against Sparta and Rome; the text identifies his audacity and weakness with the ruin of himself and the Achæans.

l: Roman Senate, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Roman Senate judged that the Lacedæmonians and Corinth should not be forced into the Achæan League, and likewise excluded Argos, Heraclea under Mount Œta, and the Arcadians of Orchomenus because they had no ancestral connection with the Achæans.

l: the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Romans sent envoys to arbitrate between the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans. Their commissioners were deceived by Critolaus and returned to Rome after failing to obtain a general meeting.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Achæans rejected the Roman decision, attacked suspected Lacedæmonians at Corinth, imprisoned those they arrested, and dismissed strangers detained on suspicion. Under Critolaus they prepared to fight Sparta and Rome, a course the text says led to their ruin.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Lacedæmonians were among the peoples whom the Roman Senate said should not be forced into the Achæan League. Lacedæmonians residing at Corinth were attacked and plundered by the Achæans, and those arrested were later imprisoned.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Thebans, encouraged by Pytheas, undertook to take an eager part in the war against the Romans. They had been heavily punished by Metellus and ordered to pay fines for invading Phocis, ravaging Eubœa, and destroying the harvest of the people of Amphissa.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Roman Senate held that the Lacedæmonians, Corinth, Argos, Heraclea under Mount Œta, and the Arcadians of Orchomenus should not be forced into the Achæan League because they lacked ancestral connection with the Achæans.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Rome sent envoys to Greece to settle the disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans. The Achæans also sent Thearidas and other prominent men as ambassadors to Rome, though they turned back after meeting other envoys on the road.

l: Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Corinth was one of the communities that the Roman Senate said should not be forced into the Achæan League. It was the place where Lacedæmonians were attacked by the Achæans and where Critolaus later collected an Achæan army.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Sparta was the target of the war that Critolaus persuaded the Achæans to undertake.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Thebes was represented by Pytheas, who was Bœotarch there and further incited the Achæans against the Romans. The Thebans agreed to participate eagerly in the war.

l: the Roman arbitration, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: The Roman arbitration held that several communities should not be compelled to remain in the Achæan League. Orestes and later Roman commissioners attempted to advance the settlement, but Critolaus obstructed the process and the commissioners returned to Rome.

l: the Lacedæmonian-Achæan disputes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Roman envoys were sent to settle the disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans. The negotiations broke down after the Achæans attacked Lacedæmonians at Corinth and Critolaus deceived the Roman commissioners.

l: the Achæan attack on the Spartans at Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: After hearing the Roman decision, the Achæans attacked all Lacedæmonians residing at Corinth, identifying some by their hair, boots, dress, or names. They plundered suspected Lacedæmonians, dragged some from Orestes’ headquarters, and later imprisoned those they had arrested.

l: war between Rome and the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIV.
s: Critolaus collected an Achæan army at Corinth and persuaded it to wage war immediately against Sparta and the Romans. Pytheas and the Thebans further encouraged the conflict, and the text says that this combination of audacity and weakness brought ruin to Critolaus and the Achæans.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Romans declared the Achæans guilty of treason and ordered Mummius to lead naval and land forces against them, while Metellus hurried to defeat them first. Critolaus rejected Metellus’ proclamation, was defeated near Scarphea, and disappeared, while Arcadian survivors were later cut to pieces at Chæronea. Diæus took command of the Achæan army, freed slaves for military service, and sent Alcamenes with 4,000 men to Megara, but Alcamenes fled to Corinth when the Romans approached. Metellus occupied Thebes and Megara and then offered the Achæans peace and harmony, but Diæus’ folly frustrated his plan.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Romans voted that the Achæans were guilty of treason and ordered Mummius to lead naval and land forces against them. Their army defeated the Arcadians at Chæronea and advanced through Boeotia and toward the Isthmus.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Achæans rejected Metellus’ proclamation, fought with Critolaus, and were defeated near Scarphea. Under Diæus they raised a new army, but their forces withdrew from Megara and their prospects for peace were frustrated by Diæus’ folly.

l: Mummius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Mummius had just been chosen consul when the Romans ordered him to lead naval and land forces against the Achæans. He set out with an army, but Metellus hurried to win the campaign before he arrived.

l: Metellus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Metellus sent a proclamation inviting the Lacedæmonians and other named cities to leave the Achæan League and promising that the Romans would not remain angry over earlier disobedience. He defeated Critolaus’ forces near Scarphea, defeated the Arcadians at Chæronea, occupied Thebes and Megara, and invited the Achæans to peace and harmony.

l: Macedonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Metellus brought his army from Macedonia and marched through Thessaly toward the Lamiac Gulf. Metellus wished to settle Macedonia and Achaia himself.

l: Achaia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Metellus wished to settle Achaia himself, but his intention was frustrated by Diæus’ folly.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Metellus ordered the Lacedæmonians and other cities named by the Romans to leave the Achæan League. Critolaus and the Achæans had also blockaded Heraclea because it would not join the League.

l: Critolaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Critolaus rejected Metellus’ peace-oriented proclamation and blockaded Heraclea with the Achæans. He fled toward Scarphea when Metellus crossed the Spercheus, and after the ensuing battle he was not seen alive or found among the dead.

l: Heraclea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Heraclea was blockaded by Critolaus and the Achæans because it would not join the Achæan League.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: About 1,000 picked Arcadian men who had fought with Critolaus marched to Elatea and were received there through old kinship. They were later met by Metellus and the Romans at Chæronea and cut to pieces, which the text presents as punishment for their earlier abandonment of Greeks fighting Philip and the Macedonians.

l: Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Chæronea was the place where Metellus and the Romans met the Arcadians returning toward the Peloponnese. The Arcadians were cut to pieces there.

l: Diæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Diæus was again made commander-in-chief of the Achæan army, freed slaves for military service, and levied Achæans and Arcadians. Despite knowing that Critolaus and the Achæan army had been defeated, he sent only 4,000 men under Alcamenes to Megara; his folly later frustrated Metellus’ plan for peace.

l: Alcamenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Alcamenes was placed in command of 4,000 men sent to garrison Megara and stop Metellus’ advance. When the Roman army approached, he and his men panicked and fled without fighting to Corinth.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Thebans had joined the Achæans in besieging Heraclea and had fought near Scarphea. When Metellus advanced, the inhabitants abandoned Thebes, but Metellus forbade his troops to burn temples, destroy buildings, or harm fugitives except Pytheas, who was captured and executed.

l: Megara, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Alcamenes and his men were sent to Megara to garrison it and halt Metellus. They fled to Corinth when the Roman army arrived, and the Megarians surrendered the town without a fight.

l: Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Alcamenes and his men fled to Corinth, where the Achæan camp was located, after abandoning Megara.

l: Roman army, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Roman army under Metellus defeated Critolaus’ forces near Scarphea, defeated the Arcadians at Chæronea, advanced to Thebes, and then marched on Megara. It did not burn Theban temples, destroy buildings, or attack fugitives other than Pytheas.

l: campaign against the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: The Romans ordered Mummius to conduct the campaign with naval and land forces, while Metellus hurried to complete it first. Metellus’ forces defeated the Achæans and their allies near Scarphea and Chæronea, occupied Thebes and Megara, and advanced to the Isthmus.

l: Metellus’ proclamation, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Metellus’ proclamation urged the Lacedæmonians and other cities named by the Romans to leave the Achæan League and promised no Roman anger over earlier disobedience. Later, at the Isthmus, he issued another proclamation inviting the Achæans to peace and harmony.

l: battle near Scarphea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Metellus’ army caught Critolaus and the Achæans during their retreat shortly before Scarphea. Many were killed and about 1,000 were captured, while Critolaus disappeared.

l: battle of Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: Metellus and the Romans met the 1,000 Arcadians returning from Elatea at Chæronea. The Romans cut the Arcadians to pieces.

l: peace and harmony between Romans and Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XV.
s: At the Isthmus, Metellus invited the Achæans to peace and harmony because he wanted to settle Macedonia and Achaia himself. Diæus’ folly prevented this intention from succeeding.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Mummius took command of the Roman army, defeated the Achæans, and captured and burned Corinth after the Achæan defeat. Diæus fled to Megalopolis, killed his wife, and took poison, while many Achæans and Corinthians escaped or were killed. Mummius destroyed the walls and arms of cities that had fought Rome, enslaved captives, and carried off Corinthian treasures. Rome then reorganized Greece, imposed taxes and political restrictions, and later remitted fines and restored some Greek institutions.

l: Mummius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Mummius took command of the Roman army, defeated the Achæans, and captured Corinth on the third day after the battle. He burned Corinth, killed many inhabitants, sold the women, children, and surviving manumitted slaves who had fought for the Achæans, removed its treasures, and destroyed the walls and arms of cities that had fought Rome. He also imposed fines and established property-based chief-magistracies after advisers arrived from Rome.

l: Roman army, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Roman army under Mummius numbered 3,500 cavalry and 22,000 infantry, with Cretan bowmen and troops brought from Attalus. It defeated the Achæans after Roman cavalry routed the opposing cavalry and 1,000 picked Roman infantry attacked the Achæan infantry from the flank.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Romans defeated the Achæans, killed many people remaining in Corinth, enslaved captives, and carried the most valuable votive offerings and ornaments to Rome. They later imposed political and financial restrictions on Greece, although they subsequently restored some institutions and remitted fines.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Achæans initially attacked the Roman advanced post and captured about 500 shields, but they were then defeated by Mummius. Their cavalry fled immediately, their infantry resisted until attacked from the flank, and many survivors fled to Corinth before escaping during the night.

l: Diæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Diæus fled toward Megalopolis as soon as the Achæans were defeated instead of defending Corinth. He announced the impending ruin of Megalopolis, killed his wife to prevent her capture, and took poison.

l: Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Corinth was left open after the battle while many Achæans and Corinthians fled. Mummius entered it with his full force on the third day, set it on fire, killed many inhabitants, sold captives, and removed its valuable offerings and ornaments.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Greece was subjected to Roman taxes, political restrictions, and the suppression of general meetings after the war. Not many years later, the Romans restored the old national meetings, allowed landholding across borders, and remitted fines imposed on Greek communities.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Rome sent Mummius and advisers to settle disputes and direct the war against the Achæans. It received the most valuable Corinthian offerings, later showed mercy to Greece by restoring institutions and remitting fines, and continued to send a prætor to govern the region.

l: Achaia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Achaia was described as the foremost Greek power through which Rome reduced Greece. The general meetings in Achaia were suppressed, and the Roman official sent to govern Greece was called the prætor of Achaia.

l: war between Rome and the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The war ended with the Roman victory over the Achæans, the destruction of Corinth, and the dismantling of the walls and arms of cities that had opposed Rome. It ended when Antitheus was Archon at Athens, in the 160th Olympiad, when Diodorus of Sicyon won the course.

l: battle between the Romans and Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: The Achæans attacked the Roman army before Mummius began the battle, but their cavalry immediately fled before the Roman cavalry. Their infantry resisted the Roman wedge-like attack until 1,000 picked Roman infantry took them in the flank and turned the battle into a complete Achæan rout.

l: Roman capture and destruction of Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVI.
s: Mummius initially avoided entering Corinth despite its open gates because he suspected an ambush. On the third day he entered with the full Roman force, burned the city, killed many of those remaining there, sold the women, children, and surviving manumitted fighters, and carried away its most valuable offerings and ornaments.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Greece suffered severe weakness and subjugation, later briefly receiving freedom from Nero before Vespasian restored taxation and Roman control. Achaia’s growth was halted by the folly of its rulers, and Dyme was plundered by Sulpicius before Augustus assigned it to Patræ. Dyme contained traditions and monuments associated with Athene, the Dindymene Mother, Attes, Sostratus, and the runner Œbotas. Œbotas’s imprecation was said to prevent Achæans from winning at Olympia until they honored him, after which Sostratus of Pellene won the boys’ race.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Greece was reduced to extreme weakness and great straits by successive disasters and conflicts. Nero later made Greece entirely free, but under Vespasian it suffered intestine discord and was again subjected to taxes and ordered to obey the prætor because, Vespasian said, Greece had unlearnt how to use liberty.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
