s: The Achæans fought a war against the Lacedæmonians. They learned through the oracle at Delphi that Œbotas’s imprecation was associated with their failure to win at Olympia, then honored him and adopted the practice of sacrificing to him before competing and crowning his statue if victorious.

l: Achaia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Achaia grew with great difficulty to considerable eminence in Greece, but the folly of its rulers stopped its growth. Its boundary with Elis was marked by the river Larisus and Dyme, and Augustus assigned Dyme to Patræ.

l: Dyme, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Dyme was an Achaean town about 30 stades from the river Larisus and the only town in Achaia that Philip the son of Demetrius reduced in war; Sulpicius consequently allowed his army to plunder it, and Augustus later assigned it to Patræ. It was formerly called Palea, and contained temples or monuments connected with Athene, the Dindymene Mother, Attes, Sostratus, and Œbotas.

l: Œbotas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Œbotas, the son of Œnias and a native of Dyme, won the foot race at the 6th Olympiad but received no special reward from the Achæans. He cursed the Achæans so that none would thereafter win at Olympia, but after they consulted Delphi and honored him, Sostratus of Pellene won the boys’ race; Achæans continued to sacrifice to Œbotas before competing and crown his statue when victorious.

l: Olympia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Olympia had a statue of Œbotas, who was later declared worthy of one by the oracle at Delphi. Achæans who intended to compete there sacrificed to Œbotas, and victorious competitors crowned his statue.

l: Attes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Attes was associated with the temple of the Dindymene Mother at Dyme, but the narrator could not ascertain who he was because the subject was a mystery. One tradition made him the son of the Phrygian Calaus and incapable of procreation; another said he was born to the daughter of the river-god Sangarius, brought up by a goat, and mutilated himself during a wedding disrupted by Agdistis.

l: Olympic victory, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVII.
s: Œbotas was the first Achæan to win an Olympic victory, taking the foot race at the 6th Olympiad. After the Achæans honored him in response to his imprecation, Sostratus of Pellene won the boys’ race.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Olenus was an originally small Achaean town near the river Pirus that was later abandoned, and its people moved to Piræ and Euryteæ. Patræ grew from the towns of Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis, was enlarged and renamed by Patreus, and later received inhabitants from other towns under Augustus. Patræ possessed the imported statue of Laphrian Artemis and celebrated Laphria with a procession and a large animal sacrifice. Ætolia and Calydon were depopulated under Augustus, while their statues and people were transferred elsewhere.

l: Olenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Olenus was an Achaean town near the river Pirus. It was originally small, but its people later abandoned it because of its weakness and moved to Piræ and Euryteæ.

l: Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Patræ developed from Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis after Patreus enlarged the walls near Aroe and gave the city his name. Its people later aided the Ætolians against the Galati, suffered severe military reverses and poverty, and were eventually augmented by inhabitants from various towns under Augustus. Patræ also received the statue of Laphrian Artemis and celebrated the festival of Laphria.

l: Aroe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Aroe was built by Eumelus under the instruction of Triptolemus, who taught him to sow corn. Patreus later enlarged the walls near Aroe to include the town within Patræ.

l: Anthea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Anthea was built jointly by Triptolemus and Eumelus and was named after Antheas, the son of Eumelus. Patreus later forbade the Achæans to settle there, and its inhabitants were among those scattered after Patræ suffered reverses.

l: Mesatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Mesatis was built between Anthea and Aroe. The people of Patræ said that Dionysus was reared there and was endangered by a plot of the Titans, and that its name had a corresponding explanation. Patreus later forbade the Achæans to settle there, and its inhabitants were among those scattered after Patræ suffered reverses.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The Achæans drove the Ionians out and later settled in the region of Patræ. The people of Patræ were the only Achæans who joined the Ætolians against the Galati; after suffering reverses and poverty, most left Patræ, while Augustus incorporated the Achæans from Rhypæ into Patræ after destroying Rhypæ.

l: Ætolia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Ætolia was depopulated by Augustus so that its people could be used to populate his city of Nicopolis near Actium. The people of Patræ had earlier joined the Ætolians in their war against the Galati.

l: Augustus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Augustus populated Nicopolis near Actium with people from Ætolia and transferred many statues from Ætolia and Acarnania there. He enlarged Patræ's population with people from various towns, destroyed Rhypæ and incorporated its Achæans into Patræ, and granted Patræ freedom and other privileges.

l: Laphrian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Laphrian Artemis was honored in the citadel of Patræ under a foreign title and with a foreign statue. The goddess's title was attributed either to Laphrius, who made the old statue, or to the lessening of Artemis's wrath against the people of Calydon.

l: Calydon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Calydon was depopulated by Augustus along with the rest of Ætolia so that Nicopolis could be populated. The people of Patræ received spoils from Calydon, including the statue of Laphrian Artemis.

l: statue of Laphrian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: The statue of Laphrian Artemis was brought from Calydon to Patræ after Augustus depopulated Calydon. It depicts the goddess as a huntress, is made of ivory and gold, and was made by Menæchmus and Soidas.

l: Laphria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XVIII.
s: Laphria was the annual festival held by the people of Patræ for Artemis. It included a procession led by a virgin priestess in a chariot drawn by stags, followed by sacrifices in which live birds, domestic and wild animals, and tree fruit were burned on a large altar.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: The Ionians of Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis worshipped Artemis Triclaria and once practiced an annual human sacrifice because Comætho and Melanippus had violated her temple through their love. After the capture of Ilium, Eurypylus son of Euæmon received a chest containing a statue of Dionysus, lost his mind upon seeing it, and was directed by the oracle at Delphi to dedicate the chest where a strange sacrifice was being offered. He arrived at Aroe during the sacrifice, and the people recognized the oracle’s meaning; Eurypylus recovered, the sacrifice ended, and the river was renamed Milichus. The people of Patras identify this Eurypylus as the son of Euæmon and sacrifice to him annually during the festival of Dionysus.

l: Eurypylus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XIX.
s: After the capture of Ilium, Eurypylus son of Euæmon received a chest containing a statue of Dionysus. He became mentally ill after opening the chest, consulted the oracle at Delphi, and was directed to dedicate it where a strange sacrifice was being offered. He arrived at Aroe, recovered when the sacrifice was stopped, and thereafter received annual sacrifices from the people of Patras during the festival of Dionysus.
